_why: A guard is proven by breaking the thing it guards and watching it go red. This project does that
and writes what the guard said into the commit message - which is real, and one-time. It cannot be
re-executed. A guard proven in one month and quietly hollowed out in the next looks exactly like a
guard that still works: the suite is green either way.
This ledger is those proofs, kept as data. Each plant is the exact text substitution that puts the
defect back, and the suite that must go RED when it is there. tools/guard/replant.py applies one,
requires the named suite to fail, restores the file byte-for-byte and verifies the restore.
THREE RATCHETS, and every one of them may only fall.
owed                 registered suites with no plant at all - the honest size of what this
ledger does not cover.
owed_generalisation  plants marked site_only: the defect was put back at exactly the place it
was found, and nothing shows the guard would catch it somewhere else.
owed_real_defect     suites whose ONLY plant is marked auto. tools/guard/autoplant.py finds
those by mutating a line and watching the suite go red, which proves the
suite is not vacuous - a real thing to know, and NOT the same claim as a
hand-written plant, where the text put back is a defect that actually
happened to a user. Kept apart so a machine-generated line can never be
mistaken for the proof it is standing in for.
PlantLedgerTest holds all three to their ceilings and checks every plant still matches its file
exactly once, which is cheap; replant.py actually runs them, which is not.

plants.why: The matrix cursor translates a point on the grid into a cell, and the multitude/sub-chunk tool makes that grid four times finer in each axis. plants.why: The NPC form wrote the zone and then re-read its script from that zone - and threw away the boolean saying whether the write had happened. plants.why: BCHFile checks its magic and returns - but only after reading a string and eleven ints out of the buffer, so bytes too short to hold a header never reach the check. Measured: decode(byte[]{1,2,3,4}) and decode(byte[0]) both die with OutOfMemoryError, which is an Error and so passes straight through a catch on Exception. One truncated region therefore took the whole editor down - from a browser whose entire job is to look at regions one after another, so it would have been found by the first person who scrolled past a bad one. Found by the guard, not by them. THE FIRST TWO DRAFTS OF THIS PLANT SURVIVED, and that was the useful part. The fix originally had two halves - this length-and-magic check and a catch on OutOfMemoryError - and each covered every input a suite could build, so neither could be proven while the other stood. No buffer could be constructed that passed the check and still ran away, so the Error catch was speculation, and speculation that cannot be tested or safely removed is worse than none. It was deleted; this check is the whole fix, and it proves. The must_say is the section wrapper's own sentence rather than a check line: an OutOfMemoryError is not a failed assertion, it is the section dying, and what this plant proves is precisely that the editor would die. The wrapper catches Throwable so it is reported rather than taking the whole battery quietly.
